ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

Acetaminophen pharmacology: 2

After excessive acetaminophen ingestion, glutathione stores become insufficient and a reactive metabolite accumulates. Which mechanism best explains the resulting liver injury rather than direct irreversible platelet inhibition or opioid receptor activation?

  1. NAPQI-mediated hepatic injury
  2. Analgesic and antipyretic effects with limited peripheral anti-inflammatory action
  3. N-acetylcysteine
  4. Unintentional duplicate acetaminophen exposure
  5. Serious cutaneous adverse reaction
Answer and explanation

NAPQI-mediated hepatic injury

Excess acetaminophen can overwhelm glutathione detoxification of the reactive metabolite NAPQI.

Option explanations

NAPQI-mediated hepatic injury: Excess acetaminophen can overwhelm glutathione detoxification of the reactive metabolite NAPQI.

Analgesic and antipyretic effects with limited peripheral anti-inflammatory action: Acetaminophen treats pain and fever but does not provide the same peripheral anti-inflammatory action as conventional NSAIDs. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

N-acetylcysteine: N-acetylcysteine supports glutathione-dependent detoxification and is the antidote used for acetaminophen poisoning. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Unintentional duplicate acetaminophen exposure: Combination cold and pain products can contain acetaminophen, creating overdose risk when totals are not reconciled. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.

Serious cutaneous adverse reaction: Acetaminophen can rarely cause severe skin reactions, including SJS/TEN; rash with blistering or mucosal injury requires urgent assessment. This does not best answer the specific question in this case.
